My experience with public healthcare is quite nice, to be honest. Appointments are made only a week ahead of time so I don't have to wait for ages, and my territory pays for airfare if I have to travel for interprovincial appointments. There are no dark hallways, plenty of staff at the three hospitals I frequent (all very helpful, especially in my beloved pacemaker wing), I always get copies of anything I ask for, particularly my ekgs and any new parameters on my ICD. My cardiologist even went back into the past decade of my biannual checkup records, all my surgery records, and all parameter changes in order to make me a package to give to a cardiologist if I have to see one while international. Proper gowns for exams, no paper, and you get one that opens each way so you can be properly covered and warm. Endless heated blankets for pre-surgery, plenty of painkillers and anti-nausea at request too which is good. Post-op, nurses will bring you crackers and jello and ice cream at any time of the day or night if you feel up to eating. They have nice bits of art and quotes and infographics on all the walls when you're trying out a little post-op walk so you don't get bored, plus dvd players and books and so on if you're stuck in bed for a few days. The only money I spend is if I choose to stay at a hotel during my checkups instead of the hospital dorms. I get to see the same doctors every time so we've had a great rapport for the past 12 years, not to mention the piece of mind knowing that no matter what my financial/work/insurance/ situation is, I will always be taken care of medically. No policies to change, no one can vote for me to have to start paying for anything, no insurance company can tell me what I can or can't have, no old white man in a suit can tell me if I'm worth saving or not, 100% security.

Unless I'm in the ER with something mild like a uti or a sprained ankle, wait times are minimal, I think the longest I ever had to wait for an appointment was 20 minutes because the patient who arrived just before me was late. They've accepted last-minute changes in case I am suddenly unable to make an appointment at all three hospitals as well. Once, one of the hospitals had a fire in the wing above my clinic, and the sprinklers flooded the clinic entirely. They simply moved my examination and several procedures to the other wing and borrowed an unused computer from pediatrics for my ICD check.

These are personal experiences, of course, I can't speak for everyone who deals with public health care. But three different hospitals with three different sets of doctors, cardiologists, and technicians in three entirely different provinces each with their own budget and their own rules, all over the course of 12 years, have been a literal lifesaver and that consistency in care quality across the west coast makes me very grateful to have public health care. I would NEVER want to change to private or anything, it would be disastrous.

I forgot to mention the free medication, aside anything like painkillers and saline and blood and whatever else you might need being free while you're checked into a hospital, even if you're just there for a couple hours in the ER you get free shit. I am always given fee painkillers and a free first dose of antibiotics if I go in for something like a UTI.

Also, communication between all three hospitals is awesome, everyone has a copy of everything and every new appointment sends updated paperwork to my interprovincial files so that everyone knows whats happening. Shit here is almost utopian compared to the states.
